title: Lesson 3: Avoiding Defensive Reactions
summary: Being corrected is not automatically an attack. Listen, examine the facts, acknowledge genuine mistakes, and explain your perspective respectfully.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Emotional maturity, accepting feedback, humility, accountability and professional communication

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a supervisor approaches a therapist at Zura Spa and says: "I noticed that the treatment room was not properly prepared before your last appointment. The clean towels were missing, and the massage oil had not been replenished."
Before the supervisor finishes speaking, the therapist responds: "But I'm not the only person who uses that room! Why are you always blaming me? What about the others?"

The supervisor attempts to explain, but the therapist continues interrupting. Eventually, the conversation becomes an argument. The original concern—ensuring the room is properly prepared—remains unresolved.

Now imagine the therapist responding differently. She listens and says: "I understand your concern. I prepared the room earlier, but I may have missed something. Could you clarify what was missing so I can address it?"
The supervisor explains the issue. The therapist discovers that she overlooked the massage oil and agrees to check the supplies more carefully before future appointments.
Both situations began with the same correction. However, the outcomes were different because one employee reacted defensively while the other remained open to understanding the feedback.
Being corrected does not automatically mean you are being attacked, and listening to feedback does not mean you must agree with every accusation.
At Zura Spa, employees should develop the maturity to hear concerns, examine the facts, acknowledge genuine mistakes and communicate their perspectives respectfully.

sections.title: 2. What is a defensive reaction?
paragraphs: A defensive reaction occurs when someone responds to perceived criticism, correction or disagreement primarily by trying to protect themselves from blame, embarrassment or discomfort.
Defensiveness may appear through words, tone, facial expressions or behaviour.
Defensiveness is a common human reaction. The objective of this lesson is not to shame employees for experiencing it but to help them recognise and manage it.
list: Interrupting before the other person finishes.
Immediately denying responsibility without considering the facts.
Blaming another employee.
Raising one's voice.
Making excuses before understanding the concern.
Bringing up unrelated past mistakes.
Responding sarcastically.
Treating every correction as a personal attack.
Refusing to acknowledge an obvious mistake.
Withdrawing from communication to avoid accountability.

sections.title: 3. Why employees become defensive

items.label: 1. Fear of blame or punishment
items.body: An employee may worry that admitting a mistake will lead to negative consequences.

items.label: 2. Embarrassment
items.body: Being corrected can feel uncomfortable, especially in front of colleagues.

items.label: 3. Personal pride
items.body: Some employees find it difficult to accept that they may have made a mistake.

items.label: 4. Perceived unfairness
items.body: An employee may believe she is being blamed for something outside her responsibility.

items.label: 5. Previous experiences
items.body: Harsh or humiliating corrections in the past may influence how someone responds to feedback.

items.label: 6. Misunderstanding
items.body: The employee may interpret a request for improvement as a judgment about her character.

paragraphs: Understanding why defensiveness occurs helps employees address the emotion without allowing it to control their response.

sections.title: 4. The difference between explaining yourself and being defensive
paragraphs: Employees have a right to explain their perspective, clarify facts and challenge inaccurate information respectfully.
The problem is not speaking up. The problem is reacting in a way that prevents understanding or accountability.
Being professional does not mean accepting blame for something you did not do. It means communicating the facts without unnecessary hostility.
table: "Could we clarify who was responsible for the task?"
"I understand the concern. Here's what I observed."
"I would appreciate specific feedback on what needs improvement."
"I was not assigned that responsibility. Can we review the arrangement?"
"My understanding of the situation is different. May I share the details?"

items.label: Communication becomes difficult
items.body: Colleagues may hesitate to raise concerns when they expect an argument.

items.label: Mistakes may be repeated
items.body: When employees focus only on defending themselves, opportunities to improve can be missed.

items.label: Relationships become strained
items.body: Repeated arguments can create resentment and reduce cooperation.

items.label: Time is wasted
items.body: Simple corrections can turn into lengthy disputes instead of practical solutions.

items.label: Service quality may suffer
items.body: Unresolved mistakes can affect room preparation, bookings, teamwork and client satisfaction.

sections.title: 6. Recognising defensive behaviour in yourself
paragraphs: Defensiveness often begins before an employee speaks.
An employee may notice certain thoughts or physical reactions.
Recognising defensiveness is the first step toward managing it.

sections.title: Common warning signs
list: Feeling an immediate urge to interrupt.
Mentally preparing a counterargument instead of listening.
Feeling that you must prove you are right.
Becoming irritated by the person's tone.
Wanting to mention someone else's mistakes.
Feeling embarrassed or threatened.
Raising your voice without intending to.
Thinking, "They are against me."
Feeling unwilling to acknowledge any part of the concern.

sections.title: Self-awareness questions
list: Am I listening to understand or only waiting to defend myself?
Do I know the complete facts?
Am I responding to the issue or reacting to how I feel?
Is there something useful I can learn?
Can I explain my perspective without attacking the other person?

sections.title: 7. Seven habits for avoiding defensive reactions
Habit 1: Allow the person to finish
paragraphs: Avoid interrupting before the concern has been fully explained.
You may discover that the feedback is different from what you initially assumed.

sections.title: Habit 2: Pause before responding
paragraphs: A brief pause can help prevent an emotional reaction.
You do not have to answer immediately.

sections.title: Habit 3: Ask clarifying questions
paragraphs: If the feedback is unclear, request specific details.
Example: "Could you explain which part of the room preparation did not meet the expected standard?"

sections.title: Habit 4: Separate the issue from your identity
paragraphs: A mistake in a task does not automatically mean you are an incompetent employee.
Feedback should focus on specific actions and outcomes.

sections.title: Habit 5: Acknowledge valid points
paragraphs: If the concern is accurate, acknowledge it.
Example: "You're right. I forgot to check the massage oil before the appointment."
Acknowledgment demonstrates accountability.

sections.title: Habit 6: Explain your perspective respectfully
paragraphs: If important information is missing, provide it calmly.
Example: "I understand the concern. I had informed reception that the towels were unavailable, but I should also have updated the supervisor."

sections.title: Habit 7: Focus on the next step
paragraphs: After understanding the issue, discuss what needs to happen.
Example: "I'll complete the room checklist before the next appointment and report any missing supplies promptly."
Key principle: You do not need to win every conversation. You need to understand the issue and help achieve the right outcome.

sections.title: 8. The difference between excuses, explanations and accountability
paragraphs: These three concepts are often confused.
An explanation is not automatically an excuse.
Employees should be able to provide relevant context without being accused of avoiding responsibility.
Likewise, employees should not use circumstances outside their control to conceal responsibilities they could reasonably have fulfilled.

items.label: Excuse
items.body: Attempts to avoid responsibility without properly addressing the issue. Example: "I didn't prepare the room because everybody was busy."

items.label: Explanation
items.body: Provides relevant facts about what happened. Example: "The room preparation was delayed because the clean towels had not arrived."

items.label: Accountability
items.body: Acknowledging the responsibility that belongs to you and taking appropriate action. Example: "The towels were delayed, but I should have informed the supervisor earlier. I'll report supply problems promptly in future."

table: Recognising responsibility and addressing the outcome

sections.title: 9. The LISTEN method for receiving correction

items.label: L — Listen completely
items.body: Allow the person to explain the concern without unnecessary interruption.

items.label: I — Identify the issue
items.body: Focus on the specific behaviour, task or outcome being discussed.

items.label: S — Stay composed
items.body: Recognise your emotions and avoid impulsive reactions.

items.label: T — Talk through the facts
items.body: Ask questions, clarify details and explain your perspective respectfully.

items.label: E — Evaluate your responsibility
items.body: Acknowledge any genuine mistake or area for improvement.

items.label: N — Next steps
items.body: Agree on an appropriate solution and follow through.

sections.title: LISTEN example
paragraphs: A receptionist is informed that an appointment was entered incorrectly.
Instead of immediately blaming another employee, she listens, checks the booking details and acknowledges the error if it was hers.
She then corrects the appointment and communicates the updated information to the relevant team members.
The goal is to resolve the booking problem and prevent it from happening again.

sections.title: 10. Avoiding defensiveness when corrected by a supervisor
paragraphs: Supervisors are responsible for helping employees understand workplace expectations.
Employees should receive legitimate corrections professionally.
However, supervisors must also communicate respectfully and fairly.
Constructive feedback is more likely to produce improvement than humiliation.

sections.title: Employee responsibilities
list: Listen attentively.
Avoid unnecessary interruptions.
Ask questions when feedback is unclear.
Acknowledge genuine mistakes.
Explain relevant facts.
Complete agreed corrective actions.

sections.title: Supervisor responsibilities
list: Explain the concern clearly.
Focus on specific behaviour or work outcomes.
Avoid personal insults.
Allow the employee to respond.
Consider relevant circumstances.
Communicate the expected improvement.
Avoid unnecessary public embarrassment.

sections.title: Example — unhelpful versus constructive correction
paragraphs: Unhelpful correction: "You are always careless. You never do anything right."

Constructive correction: "The last two room checks were incomplete. Please ensure the towels and supplies are checked before each appointment. Is there anything preventing you from completing the checklist?"

sections.title: 11. Avoiding defensiveness when corrected by colleagues
paragraphs: Not all feedback comes from management.
Colleagues may notice problems that affect shared responsibilities.
Lesson: Feedback from colleagues should be evaluated on its merits, not rejected merely because the person giving it has the same job title.

sections.title: Example — massage oil not replenished
paragraphs: A therapist tells another therapist: "The massage oil was not replenished after your session."
The second therapist may feel embarrassed.
Defensive response: "Why are you monitoring everything I do?"
Professional response: "Thank you for pointing it out. I didn't realise it was low. I'll check it before the next session."
If the employee believes the information is incorrect, she can respond: "I replenished the oil after my session. Could we check whether it was used again afterward?"

sections.title: 12. Avoiding defensiveness when clients complain
paragraphs: Client complaints may feel personal, particularly when employees have worked hard.
However, employees should distinguish between receiving a complaint and being personally attacked.
Employees should listen carefully, acknowledge the concern and follow appropriate service and reporting procedures.
They should not make promises they are not authorised to fulfil.

sections.title: Example — pressure too firm
paragraphs: A client says: "The massage pressure was too firm even after I asked for it to be reduced."
Defensive response: "That's how Deep Tissue Massage works. You should have booked something else."
Professional response: "I'm sorry the pressure was not adjusted to your preference. Thank you for explaining your experience. I'll ensure the concern is reported appropriately."

sections.title: 13. What if the correction is unfair or inaccurate?
paragraphs: Avoiding defensiveness does not mean accepting every statement as true.
Employees may sometimes receive feedback based on incomplete information.
The appropriate response is to clarify the facts respectfully.
Employees should not be pressured into admitting wrongdoing they did not commit.
Maturity means being willing to accept valid correction and equally willing to clarify inaccurate information respectfully.

sections.title: Example — room used after preparation
paragraphs: A supervisor accuses a therapist of failing to prepare a room.
However, the therapist had already completed the preparation and another employee used the room afterward.
Unprofessional response: "You don't know what you're talking about!"

Professional response: "I understand why the room's condition is concerning. I completed the preparation at 1 p.m., but the room was used afterward. Could we review the timeline before deciding what happened?"

sections.title: Appropriate steps
list: Listen to the concern.
Identify any factual disagreement.
Explain your perspective calmly.
Provide relevant information or evidence.
Request a fair review.
Escalate appropriately if the issue cannot be resolved.

sections.title: 14. When defensiveness turns into blame-shifting
paragraphs: Blame-shifting occurs when someone attempts to transfer responsibility to another person instead of addressing their own role.
Accountability does not require taking responsibility for everything. It requires taking responsibility for the part that genuinely belongs to you.

sections.title: Example — an appointment change not communicated
paragraphs: A receptionist forgets to inform a therapist about an appointment change.
When questioned, she says: "The therapist should have checked the schedule herself."
The therapist may indeed have responsibilities relating to the schedule. However, that does not automatically remove the receptionist's responsibility to communicate the change.
Better response: "I did not communicate the change promptly. I understand that this affected the therapist's preparation. I'll ensure future changes are communicated as soon as they are confirmed."

sections.title: Case study A: The defensive therapist
paragraphs: A supervisor corrects a therapist for failing to replenish treatment-room supplies.
The therapist immediately says: "Everybody uses that room. Why are you blaming only me?"
Expected lesson: Employees should seek clarification before reacting and acknowledge responsibilities supported by the facts.
list: What triggered the defensive reaction?
What facts might need clarification?
How could the therapist respond more professionally?
What should the supervisor do to ensure fairness?
What would an appropriate resolution look like?

sections.title: Case study B: The receptionist who made a mistake
paragraphs: A receptionist enters an incorrect appointment time.
When the mistake is discovered, she blames the client for giving confusing information.
Later, the booking record shows that the client provided the correct time.
Expected lesson: Accountability requires acknowledging genuine errors and taking corrective action.
list: What defensive behaviour occurred?
Why is blame-shifting harmful?
What should the receptionist acknowledge?
How can the mistake be corrected?
What procedure could prevent a recurrence?

sections.title: Case study C: The colleague's feedback
paragraphs: A therapist politely tells another therapist that the room was not fully cleaned after the previous session.
The employee becomes offended and refuses to speak to her colleague.
Expected lesson: Employees should evaluate feedback without automatically treating it as hostility.
list: Why might the employee feel embarrassed?
How did defensiveness affect teamwork?
What would be a more constructive response?
How can colleagues give feedback respectfully?

sections.title: Case study D: The inaccurate accusation
paragraphs: An employee is accused of failing to complete a task.
She has evidence showing that the task was completed and the issue occurred afterward.
Expected lesson: Avoiding defensiveness includes communicating accurate information respectfully, not accepting false blame.
list: Should the employee accept blame to avoid conflict?
How can she explain the facts professionally?
What should the supervisor do before reaching a conclusion?
How can the situation be resolved fairly?

sections.title: 16. Practical group activity: Replace the defensive response
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise receiving feedback without unnecessary defensiveness.
Divide participants into pairs. One person gives feedback, and the other practises responding professionally.
Expected outcome: Participants should learn to receive feedback with openness, accuracy and respect.
table: "Could we clarify the facts and responsibilities?"
"I understand the concern. I'll review what happened."
"I would appreciate specific feedback on what needs improvement."
"Could we confirm who was assigned this responsibility?"
"Please, explain the concern so I can understand it."

sections.title: Role-play exercise
list: The supervisor identifies a missed room-preparation step.
The employee listens without interrupting.
The employee asks a clarifying question.
The employee acknowledges any genuine responsibility.
Both agree on an appropriate next step.

sections.title: 17. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 3 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is a defensive reaction? A respectful explanation of relevant facts / A response focused mainly on protecting oneself from perceived blame or criticism / A willingness to accept constructive feedback

A supervisor corrects your work. What is the most professional first response? Listen fully and seek clarification where necessary / Immediately blame another employee / Raise your voice to defend yourself
Which statement demonstrates accountability? Everybody else makes mistakes too. / It's never my responsibility. / I missed that step. I'll correct it and follow the procedure next time.

What should an employee do if a correction is inaccurate? Accept blame even when the facts are wrong / Explain the facts respectfully and request clarification or review / Insult the person giving the correction

What does the LISTEN method encourage? Listening, identifying the issue, staying composed, discussing facts, evaluating responsibility and agreeing on next steps / Avoiding every difficult conversation / Responding immediately before hearing the full concern

sections.title: 18. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what a defensive reaction means in the workplace.
Identify five reasons employees may become defensive when receiving correction.
Describe three ways defensive reactions can negatively affect teamwork.
Explain the difference between an excuse, an explanation and accountability.
Describe the LISTEN method in your own words.
Explain how you would respond if a supervisor corrected you for a genuine mistake.
Describe how you would respond if you were wrongly accused of failing to complete a task.
Explain why accepting feedback does not mean accepting every accusation.
Identify three defensive habits you would like to improve.
Describe how supervisors and employees can work together to make feedback more constructive.

sections.title: 19. Seven-day feedback challenge
table: Notice when you feel the urge to defend yourself
Ask a clarifying question when receiving feedback
Acknowledge one genuine area for improvement
Explain your perspective without blaming others
Focus on solutions rather than winning an argument
Reflect on how your response to feedback has improved

sections.title: 20. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Defensive reactions are common, especially when employees feel embarrassed, misunderstood or unfairly criticised.
However, employees can learn to manage these reactions.
At Zura Spa, receiving correction should not automatically lead to arguments, excuses, blame-shifting or withdrawal.
Employees should listen carefully, clarify facts, acknowledge genuine mistakes and communicate their perspectives respectfully.
Supervisors should also provide feedback fairly, clearly and without unnecessary humiliation.
Next topic: Accepting Corrections and Constructive Feedback with Humility.

remember: You do not become a better employee by proving that you are never wrong. You become better by being willing to learn, acknowledge mistakes and improve. At the same time, maturity does not require accepting false blame. At Zura Spa, professionalism means listening with an open mind, speaking with respect and focusing on what is true, fair and helpful. Do not allow defensiveness to prevent your growth or damage your relationships with others.
